<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with disciplined, closed-book reasoning and clear A1:/A2: compliance. PRO built a coherent case (act inside the window, bounded escalation, destroyed cascades) and landed two genuinely strong counterpunches: the "window" reframe that defused CON's alleged contradiction, and the closing turn that CON's "unspent threat" was in fact evaporating leverage while Iran climbed to 60% and stripped cameras. But CON isolated PRO's load-bearing forward claim — "every step of that path is detectable and strikeable" — and never let it go, exposing the mortgage-on-a-spent-asset problem. CON's best original move, "monitoring never had to find the hidden room; it had to make the hidden room necessary," reframed the transparency loss from passive watching into an active cost-imposing mechanism, which blunted PRO's strongest attack on the value of inspections. CON also kept a single consistent metric (price per unit of time, ledger a decade out) and PRO's honest but exploitable concession ("buried, or in a warehouse... in both cases" fine) handed CON its cleanest closing hook. PRO won the escalation-risk axis and answered the contradiction charge well, but its case increasingly depended on future detection capability that CON credibly showed the strikes degraded. PRO also incurred two clipped speeches, costing it the end of its opening burden-setting and its second rebuttal's final weighing. Clear but competitive win for CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B2.1]: "You cannot mock the scoreboard and then promise to keep score after you've thrown it out," aimed squarely at PRO's [A2.4] claim that every covert step is detectable and strikeable. PRO's reply (Fordow was found by intelligence, not inspectors) was plausible and partially effective, but CON's follow-up — that accounting loss lets Iran divert declared material with no discrepancy, and that HUMINT/procurement collection is hardest in a just-struck, purged regime — kept the pressure alive through the closing.</best_rebuttal>
